title: Luka Saxena
text:
Current Role
I’m a Research Associate at The George Institute for Global Health, embedded in the Critical Care team. My primary project is SEPSIS SUPPORT – an NHMRC-funded program co-designing the first targeted models of post-sepsis care in Australia. Sepsis affects around 55,000 Australians each year, yet support after hospital discharge remains critically limited. The project brings together survivors, clinicians, and caregivers to change that.

title: Luka Saxena
text:
Goals & Aspirations


MSc Health Data Science
Building a rigorous foundation in statistical modelling, machine learning, and reproducible research through my Masters at UNSW – and writing about what I learn along the way.


Applying Skills in the Field
Taking what I learn directly into live research at The George Institute – developing the data infrastructure, analysis pipelines, and visualisations that drive SEPSIS SUPPORT forward.


Towards a PhD
Developing ideas at the intersection of health data science and critical care research, with a longer-term goal of pursuing a PhD that bridges both.

title: Welcome To My Blog
text:
Hi, I’m Luka. Thanks for stopping by. This is a small corner of the internet where I plan to think out loud about working with data. I’ve started it for a simple reason: I’m learning a lot right now, and I wanted somewhere to keep track of it all, share the good bits, and look back later on how far I’ve come.
By day I work in health and medical research, and on the side I’m studying health data science. This blog is where I’ll share my journey as it actually unfolds: the things I’m learning, the problems I get stuck on, and the small wins that make everything click into place.
A few things you can expect to find here:

Notes from my growth as a data scientist, and how I’m getting there
Fun data tips, tricks, and shortcuts I wish I’d known sooner
Visualisations and experiments, the prettier side of working with data
Honest reflections on finding my way in this field and building a career in it

I’m also writing this partly for myself. Think of it as a personal repository for the cool things I pick up along the way, the kind of stuff that’s too good to forget but too easily lost in a tangle of bookmarks and half-remembered tutorials. If it ends up helping you too, even better. So have a look around. A lot of this is still a work in progress, and that’s exactly the point. Come back now and then to see what’s new.
Thanks for reading,
Luka

title: PRISMA2020 on R
text:
If you have ever put together a systematic review, you will know the PRISMA flow diagram: that box-and-arrow chart showing how many records you found, screened, excluded, and finally included. For a long time I thought you could only manually build this in word or canva, nudging boxes around and re-typing numbers every time a count changed. It worked, but it was fiddly and very easy to get wrong.
Then I found the PRISMA2020 R package, and it changed how I do this completely. Here is how I got it working, including where to find the template and the actual code I used.


PRISMA2020 was built by Haddaway and colleagues to produce flow diagrams that follow the PRISMA 2020 standard. You fill in a simple CSV with your record counts, point R at it, and the package draws the whole diagram for you. You can output a static image, or an interactive HTML version where each box carries a tooltip or a hyperlink.



Install it from CRAN:
install.packages("PRISMA2020")
library(PRISMA2020)
To locate the bundled template and see where it lives on your machine:
csvFile <- system.file("extdata", "PRISMA.csv", package = "PRISMA2020")
csvFile   # prints the full path so you can open and copy it
Open that file, save a copy into your project, and fill in your own numbers.



The template is one row of data with a column for each number the diagram needs: records from databases and registers, records from other sources such as citation searching and websites, duplicates removed, records screened and excluded, reports sought and not retrieved, and so on.
For my review the records came in from seven different sources, so I made sure each one landed in the right column before reading the file back into R.



Once the CSV was filled in, the rest was short:
# Read in my filled-in template
data <- read.csv("data/prisma.csv")

# Convert it into the structure the package expects
data <- PRISMA_data(data)

# Build the diagram
plot <- PRISMA_flowdiagram(
  data,
  fontsize    = 12,
  interactive = FALSE,   # set TRUE for an interactive HTML version
  previous    = FALSE,   # I had no previous-version arm
  other       = TRUE     # I did have "other" sources, so keep this on
)

plot

PRISMA_save(plot, filename = "prisma_flowdiagram.png", filetype = "PNG")
Two arguments are worth knowing, because they caught me out at first. previous controls the left-hand arm for studies carried over from an earlier version of the review, and other controls the arm for records found through methods other than database searching. If your diagram looks off or has empty boxes, these two toggles are usually the culprit.



Here is the finished diagram for my review:

title: Making a Sankey diagram in R
text:
I work on SEPSIS SUPPORT, a research program at The George Institute looking at care after sepsis. Part of that work involved looking through existing research to compare sepsis survivors with general ICU survivors, and the types of care each group receives.
I needed one figure that showed, for each patient group, which interventions they received, how those interventions fit into broader categories, and where the evidence came from. Stacked bars couldn’t show all of that at once. A Sankey diagram could: each band links a patient group to an intervention, its width shows how often that happens, and colour carries the extra information.






Important



The interventions and numbers below are made up for this post. They are not results from any real study.

title: Making a Sankey diagram in R
Making a Sankey diagram in R
text:
1. The data
Each row is an intervention, its category, and a count for every combination of patient group and study origin.

interventions <- tribble(
  ~intervention,              ~category,                     ~sepsis_aus, ~sepsis_int, ~general_aus, ~general_int,
  "Follow-up clinic",         "Body Functions & Structures",  1,           8,           3,            40,
  "Psychology review",        "Body Functions & Structures",  1,           6,           2,            35,
  "Physiotherapy assessment", "Body Functions & Structures",  0,           5,           2,            30,
  "Medication check",         "Body Functions & Structures",  0,           4,           1,            18,
  "Exercise program",         "Activities & Participation",   1,           5,           2,            32,
  "Education resources",      "Activities & Participation",   1,           7,           2,            28,
  "Telehealth check-in",      "Contextual Factors",           0,           3,           3,            25,
  "Care coordination",        "Contextual Factors",           1,           4,           2,            22,
  "Peer support group",       "Contextual Factors",           0,           2,           1,            12,
  "Carer support",            "Contextual Factors",           0,           1,           1,             6,
  "Other",                    "Other",                        0,           2,           1,            15
)

Reshape to one row per flow, and drop any zero counts.

flows <- interventions |>
  pivot_longer(
    sepsis_aus:general_int,
    names_to = c("patient_group", "origin"),
    names_sep = "_",
    values_to = "n"
  ) |>
  filter(n > 0) |>
  mutate(
    patient_group = recode(patient_group,
                           sepsis  = "Sepsis survivors",
                           general = "General critical illness"),
    origin = recode(origin, aus = "Australian", int = "International")
  )

title: Making a Sankey diagram in R
text:
2. Nodes and links
Nodes are the two patient groups on the left and the interventions on the right. The “(n=…)” in each label is calculated from the data, so it always matches.

totals <- flows |> count(intervention, wt = n)

nodes <- bind_rows(
  tibble(key   = c("Sepsis survivors", "General critical illness"),
         name  = key,
         group = "Patient group"),
  interventions |>
    left_join(totals, by = "intervention") |>
    transmute(key   = intervention,
              name  = paste0(intervention, " (n=", n, ")"),
              group = category)
)

links <- flows |>
  mutate(
    source = match(patient_group, nodes$key) - 1,  # networkD3 counts from 0
    target = match(intervention,  nodes$key) - 1
  )

title: Making a Sankey diagram in R
text:
3. Colours
Node colours show the category, and link colours show study origin. I define them once in R and build the D3 colour scale from them, so the plot and legend always agree.

node_cols <- c(
  "Patient group"               = "#5B5B5B",
  "Body Functions & Structures" = "#3FBFB8",
  "Activities & Participation"  = "#FFD54F",
  "Contextual Factors"          = "#9A6FB0",
  "Other"                       = "#C5DCDC"
)

origin_cols <- c(
  "Australian"    = "#F4A6D7",
  "International" = "#A8E4E0"
)

all_cols <- c(node_cols, origin_cols)

colour_scale <- htmlwidgets::JS(sprintf(
  "d3.scaleOrdinal().domain(%s).range(%s)",
  jsonlite::toJSON(names(all_cols)),
  jsonlite::toJSON(unname(all_cols))
))

title: Making a Sankey diagram in R
text:
4. Draw

sankey <- sankeyNetwork(
  Links       = as.data.frame(links),
  Nodes       = as.data.frame(nodes),
  Source      = "source",
  Target      = "target",
  Value       = "n",
  NodeID      = "name",
  NodeGroup   = "group",
  LinkGroup   = "origin",
  colourScale = colour_scale,
  fontSize    = 13,
  fontFamily  = "Arial",
  nodeWidth   = 28,
  nodePadding = 10,
  width       = 1000,
  height      = 750,
  sinksRight  = FALSE,
  iterations  = 0
)

# networkD3 has no built-in legend, so add one underneath with HTML
legend_item <- function(label, colour) {
  tags$span(
    style = "display:inline-flex; align-items:center; margin-right:24px;",
    tags$span(style = sprintf(
      "width:14px; height:14px; margin-right:6px; background:%s;", colour
    )),
    label
  )
}

legend <- tags$div(
  style = "font: 13px Arial; margin-top: 10px;",
  tags$b("Study origin:"),
  tags$div(style = "margin: 6px 0 12px;",
           Map(legend_item, names(origin_cols), origin_cols)),
  tags$b("Node colour (ICF category):"),
  tags$div(style = "margin-top: 6px;",
           Map(legend_item, names(node_cols), node_cols))
)

sankey <- htmlwidgets::appendContent(sankey, legend)
sankey



Study origin:



Australian



International


Node colour (ICF category):



Patient group



Body Functions & Structures



Activities & Participation



Contextual Factors

title: Making a Sankey diagram in R
text:
5. Export

htmlwidgets::saveWidget(sankey, "sankey.html", selfcontained = TRUE)

webshot2::webshot("sankey.html", "sankey.png",
                  vwidth = 1100, vheight = 900, zoom = 3)

title: Making a Sankey diagram in R
text:
Tips and tricks

Colour links by a third variable. LinkGroup lets the bands carry extra information (here, study origin) on top of the nodes they connect.
Split one flow into several links. Each patient group and intervention pair has one link per origin, which is how you get the thin pink band sitting on top of the teal one.
Lock the order with iterations = 0. Nodes appear in the order you define them, so grouping interventions by category in your data keeps the colours together on the plot.
Calculate labels from the data. Building “(n=…)” with paste0() means your labels can never disagree with your numbers.
Drop zero counts. Zero-width links can cause odd gaps, so filter them out first.
Add a legend with appendContent(). networkD3 doesn’t draw one, but you can attach any HTML underneath the widget, and it carries through to saveWidget().
Give it room. Wide Sankeys get squashed in a blog column, so #| column: page lets the plot use the full page width.
